title: Two lines and a container
spec: MCP03 · migrating one server from stdio to HTTP
intro: The same three tools, the same file, the same behaviour. What changes is who can reach them: a subprocess only your machine can spawn becomes a URL your whole team can point at. Four steps, and only one of them touches server code.

provenance.source: a narrated migration of MCP01's document_server.py using the code, Dockerfile and client config shipped in the MCP03 lab; terminal output is reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: MCP03 Lab — steps 1–5, then docker stop mcp-lab && docker rm mcp-lab.

steps.title: Swap the transport
narrative: Open document_server.py from MCP01. The tools do not move, the decorators do not change, the schemas Claude sees are identical. The only required edit is the last two lines.

mcp.run() with no arguments means stdio: read JSON-RPC frames on stdin, write them to stdout, and die when the parent process does. transport="streamable-http" starts a real HTTP server instead — which is why host and port suddenly matter, and why they come from environment variables rather than being hardcoded.
0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1 is not carelessness: inside a container, binding to loopback makes the server unreachable from the host even with -p published.
steps.youDo: Delete mcp.run(), add the streamable-http block, then python document_server.py and curl http://localhost:8000/health.

steps.title: Put it in a container that can prove it's alive
narrative: The Dockerfile is deliberately dull except for one line. HEALTHCHECK makes the container assert its own liveness by calling the endpoint you just curled — so docker ps reports healthy or unhealthy instead of the useless Up 4 minutes a crashed-inside process would also show.
The two ENV lines are what make the environment-variable defaults from step 1 pay off: the same image runs on port 8000 locally and on whatever port a platform hands you, with no rebuild.
COPY requirements.txt before COPY document_server.py is not stylistic either — it keeps the pip install layer cached across every server edit you make.
steps.youDo: docker build -t mcp-lab . then docker run -d --name mcp-lab -p 8000:8000 mcp-lab && curl http://localhost:8000/health.

before.title: THE IMAGE — the HEALTHCHECK is the line that matters

view.text: Under stdio there was nothing to health-check — the server only existed while a client held it open, so "is it up?" was not a question you could ask. An HTTP server has a lifetime of its own, which is the upgrade and also the new thing you have to babysit.

steps.title: Flip the client config
narrative: This is the whole migration from the client's side. The stdio block told the client how to start a process: an interpreter, a script path, and an environment for it. The HTTP block tells it where to connect: a URL.
Everything downstream is unchanged. The tool list, the schemas, the JSON-RPC method names, the way Claude decides to call search_documents — none of it knows which of these two blocks it came from.

Toggle Before / After. Notice what disappears: absolute paths, PYTHONPATH, and the requirement that every teammate have Python and your dependencies installed. Notice what appears: a hostname you now have to keep running.
steps.youDo: Edit .claude/settings.json in your project root and replace the command/args block with the url block.

before.title: BEFORE — stdio: how to start a subprocess

view.note: Every teammate needs this path to exist on their own disk, with the right interpreter and the right dependencies.
No auth headers for a local-only dev server. In production this grows a "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${MCP_TOKEN}"} block — which is the first bill HTTP hands you.

steps.title: What the URL costs you
narrative: The migration worked and the tools are identical — so it is tempting to read HTTP as the grown-up transport and stdio as the training-wheels one. It is not that clean.

stdio has no auth story because it does not need one: the client spawns the process, so trust is inherited from the OS. The moment you publish a port you own authentication, CORS, TLS, and the reverse-proxy trap this module spends a whole quiz question on — nginx buffers responses by default, which silently queues SSE events until you set proxy_buffering off. None of those failure modes existed an hour ago.

So pick on reach, not on sophistication. One developer, one machine, one server → stdio, and skip the container entirely. A server several people or several hosts must share → HTTP, and budget for the operational surface that comes with it.

view.text: Two lines of Python and one config block is genuinely the whole code migration — the module is not overselling that. What it cannot make small is the operational surface on the other side. Move to HTTP when sharing is the requirement; staying on stdio is not a lesser answer when nobody else needs the server.
